title: Construction management system, from tender to warranty
summary: Construction projects worth millions often run on Excel and WhatsApp. Together with a contracting company, I built a system where the office and the crew work on the same data.

facts.label: Scope
facts.value: Office panel and a mobile app for the crew

coverAlt: Comparing a subcontractor's quote with the cost estimate in Voltiq
coverNote: The interface is in Polish because Voltiq is built for Polish contractors.

problem.title: The problem
problem.text: Friday, 5 pm. A site manager calls subcontractors one by one to find out how much they have really done, because Monday's progress report is due. The estimate lives in Excel, tasks live in phones, and site photos get lost in chat.

sections.title: The estimate becomes the source of truth
sections.text: The tender estimate from the investor's Excel file goes into the system and defines the scope and value of the project. Nobody retypes it by hand.
sections.imageAlt: Tender table imported from an Excel file

sections.title: The site runs from a phone
sections.text: The crew sees their tasks, uploads photos and reports progress on site. Subcontractors quote through a plain link with no account, because every required login kills adoption on site.
sections.imageAlt: Task list with an assigned contractor and site manager

sections.title: Billing follows the work
sections.text: The progress report is calculated from what was reported on site. Completion and value appear automatically, so billing no longer starts with a round of phone calls.
sections.imageAlt: Progress report with automatically calculated value

results.label: phone photos in one site survey task
cost items loaded from the investor's Excel

decisionsTitle: Three decisions from the Voltiq project

decisions.title: Every login costs you adoption
decisions.text: A subcontractor won't create an account to send a quote, so a plain link is enough.

decisions.title: The crew is harder to win over than the office
decisions.text: People on site decide whether a rollout works, so the mobile app is the core, not an add-on.

decisions.title: The product comes from the work, not the spec
decisions.text: Every feature started from a problem on a specific site, not from market analysis.

title: Changing a tenant without guessing what to click
summary: Comgy provides energy data for buildings. Property managers got lost during a simple tenant change, so I rebuilt that flow screen by screen around one obvious action.

facts.label: Way of working
facts.value: More than 8 six-week Shape Up cycles

coverAlt: Comgy panel with tenant history and a change tenant button

problem.title: The problem
problem.text: A manager has to keep tenant data up to date and send tenants consumption information. With many apartments it is easy to get lost: it was unclear whether to edit the current tenant or add a new one, and installer shortcuts were mixed with manager actions.

sections.title: Starting point
sections.text: I joined Comgy after two designers had left and there was no established way of doing design work. I was responsible for two areas: the tenant portal, which shows consumption and CO₂ emissions, and the part of the management portal for people who handle tenants. The company worked in Shape Up cycles: every six weeks a team with a PM, a tester, 3–4 developers and a designer gets one well-described problem.

sections.title: The task first, then the screen
sections.text: With the product manager I reviewed the existing solution and user reports. We described a simple persona: a manager with many apartments who gets lost in the current system. On a problem canvas I gathered the goal, success metric, context, tasks, opportunities and risks, and turned the tasks into user stories and a flow.
sections.imageAlt: Problem canvas for changing a tenant

lesson: Beyond the flow itself, we introduced UX standards such as user flows and user tests. Working with a different team every six weeks also taught me to adapt quickly to new requirements.

walkthrough.title: One task, seven screens
walkthrough.intro: I checked the old and the new flow against the same manager task:
walkthrough.task: Move out tenant Max Mustermann from apartment EG rechts at Berlinerallee 52.

steps.title: List of buildings
steps.problem: Buildings on the left, installer parameters on the right with abbreviations (HCA, HM) that managers don't know.
steps.solution: Installer actions moved to a dedicated page. Managers see only what they can do.

steps.title: Building details
steps.problem: You can't change the tenant at this level. It is also unclear whether to edit the current tenant or add a new one, and editing would overwrite the history.
steps.solution: The menu gets “Change tenant”. There are two forms, move-in and move-out, and the system picks the right one based on the tenant's status.

steps.title: Apartment details
steps.problem: No primary action. It isn't clear where a tenant change starts.
steps.solution: A primary “Change tenant” button sits at the top. Users don't have to remember whether it is a move-in or a move-out.

steps.title: Wizard: move-out
steps.problem: Every field was active, including ones that make no sense for a move-out.
steps.solution: Values that matter for the decision stay visible but are disabled.

steps.title: Wizard: portal access
steps.problem: Portal access was asked about during a move-out, though it only makes sense for a move-in.
steps.solution: The question appears only when editing or moving in. A reminder at the top shows the previous tenant and the apartment's condition, with communication below.

steps.title: Last step
steps.problem: At the end you had to decide whether to add the next tenant. Leaving this screen cancelled every change.
steps.solution: The process ends here. You can close the screen or add the next tenant, and nothing is lost.

steps.title: Notification
steps.problem: The notification after the change said nothing useful.
steps.solution: The notification says who replaced whom, so you can see right away that the result is correct.

afterSections.title: Corridor tests
afterSections.text: We showed the new approach to a few managers. They understood it quickly and saw straight away that it would shorten learning the system and their daily work.

afterSections.title: Implementation
afterSections.text: I met developers three times a week. When something was missing or would take too long, I redesigned it on the spot. At the end I did the final check and approved the result.

quote.text: Working together with Krzysztof means being on a journey to understand your users, the use cases and their pains.
quote.name: Franziska Kaiser

title: Schedules for trainers: from interviews to the first paid licences
summary: Calenday set out to shorten schedule planning for personal trainers. I ran the project from the first conversations, through two product versions, to marketing and the first paid licences. After two years my partner and I froze the project.

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Frozen after two years of development

coverAlt: Trainer's weekly schedule in Calenday with an SMS conversation about moving a session

problem.title: The problem
problem.text: Trainers spend about two hours a week organising their calendars, and clients often move sessions. A perfect schedule quickly turns into a fragmented plan full of gaps.

sections.title: Where the idea came from
sections.text: I train with personal trainers regularly and noticed how much clients constantly rescheduling wore them down. After talking to one of them, I decided it was a serious problem and started researching it. Over time I convinced Antoine, an investor and developer, to join the project.
sections.imageAlt: A trainer's weekly schedule with gaps after rescheduled sessions

sections.title: 16 interviews in two rounds
sections.text: I listed local trainers and met them. After a few conversations the same problems kept coming up. After the second round I asked whether they would use such a solution, and most said yes. I also mapped the whole booking process, gathered the conclusions on a Lean Canvas and checked every new idea against it.

sections.title: The first version didn't work
sections.text: The idea was simple: clients share their available hours, the system builds the week, the trainer accepts it and clients get invitations. Tests showed the problem was in the details. Trainers got control over everything and ended up spending more time on setup than before, and nobody understood the alternative time proposals. Performance was another issue: above 30 sessions a week every change took 30–45 seconds to recalculate.
sections.imageAlt: First version of Calenday with the alternative proposals dialog

sections.title: Second version: automation
sections.text: Users said one thing: everything takes too long. Automation became the main principle. At the start of working with a client, the trainer sets fixed slots and flexible ranges, and the system proposes times on its own. That combination simplified the idea and solved the performance problem.
sections.imageAlt: Setting fixed training slots for a client

lesson: Many new smart-calendar startups appeared, including AI-based ones, so after two years we froze the project. I learned marketing and sales, how to lead a team, and how to get the most out of a limited budget.

decisions.title: Smart queue
decisions.text: When someone cancels, the system puts a client from the queue in their place as a proposal. The trainer only accepts it.

decisions.title: Session packages
decisions.text: Trainers see how many sessions are left in each package, and the system reminds them when a package is running out.

decisions.title: Answers from text messages
decisions.text: Google Natural Language recognises clients' replies, so “I can't” or “works for me” updates the schedule without manual clicks.

afterSections.title: The algorithm on diagrams
afterSections.text: To fix performance, I agreed with the developer that I would draw how the algorithm should work. I made many diagrams covering every situation, including the unusual ones. That made the algorithm easier to build, and I knew nothing had been missed.
afterSections.imageAlt: Block diagram for sending a text message
